RagShortTexts: Sour soups use available greens and souring agents; dairy and meat depend on means and fasts.
Soup needs water, fuel and vessels, and a shared name does not ensure one recipe.

Variants.Content:
A household sour soup may combine garden vegetables, edible wild greens and available souring ingredients, with bread or porridge to feed several people. Stored sour greens, fermented grain liquor or other sour ingredients give different flavours, and cooks adapt to supplies. Meat stock and dairy depend on animals, money and the religious calendar; a rich table does not establish what an inn or poor home serves.

A pot also requires water, split wood, cleaning and someone to watch the fire. Dry fuel and an intact vessel can determine when hot food is ready in bad weather. Soured milk and milk fat accompany other foods, subject to storage and preference. Children, elders and sick people may need softer portions and help with eating, taking time from other work.
An estate feast and workers’ meal use different resources: one pot of soup can hide very different meat, grain and fuel costs. Fasts also require meals without meat or dairy.
Hot soup on the road needs a halt, a pot and fuel. Softening dry food helps those with poor teeth or injuries, but water and remaining rations still need accounting.
Cooks may save scarce rich ingredients for guests or sick people while grain fills most stomachs. Exchanging sour greens or dairy with neighbours adds variety and creates obligations.
